vignette: Elias Vance had always trusted his training and the men who shared his hangar. That certainty fractured during a layover in Germany, when a senior officer he had flown alongside for years turned his quiet hospitality into something calculated and violating. Elias could still feel the suffocating shift in the room, the way the familiar routine of the base suddenly curdled into something entirely unpredictable, and the deliberate dismantling of the respect he had placed in the man's hands. The betrayal was not merely a single moment; it rewired how he read the world. He began to interpret every glance and hesitation around him as a precursor to danger, his mind clinging to the terrifying certainty that he had been fundamentally deceived by someone he had relied on. This conviction did not stay abstract. The more he judged himself as broken, as a lousy coper who could not even protect his own boundaries, the more his eyes began to hunt for signs of duplicity in every crowded terminal and briefing room. When colleagues paused mid-sentence or changed their routes without explanation, Elias's breath would catch, his shoulders hiking toward his ears, convinced he was walking into another ambush. Back in the Nevada desert, the cockpit that once demanded his absolute focus now amplified his distress. Sudden schedule scrambles no longer read as standard operational tempo; they felt like the ground giving way beneath his boots. He had come to believe he had lost all faith in the structures meant to keep him safe, both on the ground and in the air. This erosion of trust directly fed his physiology. Every time he braced for the next blow, his heart hammered against his ribs, his body primed and ready to react before a threat even materialized. He would jump at the mundane click of a radio or the heavy tread of a ground crewman walking behind his chair. He spent hours after shift lying in bed, his head tilted toward the hallway, listening for the faintest scrape of a door handle or the whisper of footsteps that might mean someone was entering his apartment. He felt perpetually on guard, even within his own walls, as if the enemy had learned his address. His body's relentless readiness slowly poisoned his daily routine. The constant startle responses made him miss critical briefings, and his need to verify every exit in a room drew sharp looks from his flight surgeon. Over the months, these reactions did not fade; they hardened into a quiet desperation. He was certain that his own reactions since the event proved he was fundamentally failing, and that the world outside his airman's quarters offered no genuine sanctuary. The tighter his chest constricted, the more his body flinched at ordinary shifts in routine, and the more he expected unpredictability to strike from any blind corner. He had tried to push through the drills, but the physical toll and the emotional isolation had become unsustainable. What finally brought him to the clinic was the morning he realized he could no longer look at his co-pilot without bracing for a violation, and that his own hands would tremble too badly to keep the jet level. He was seeking a way to quiet the constant alarm in his chest, hoping to find a place where he could finally lower his guard without feeling like he was walking into another trap.
